common_name: Rotkopf Hens and Chicks (Kohlein Red-Tipped Houseleek Hybrid)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto the surface of lean, fast-draining soil in spring or fall; this cultivar tolerates more winter wet than many sempervivums but still needs sharp drainage.

directions: 'Rotkopf' was bred in 1962 by Dr. Fritz Kohlein, crossing Sempervivum tectorum with S. marmoreum, and has since earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Its spatula-shaped, gray-green leaves are rimmed in deep red to maroon and intensify to near solid red in strong sun, forming tight rosettes that spread steadily on short stolons. Clusters of starry pink flowers rise on 6-8 inch stems in summer, after which the flowering rosette dies back while surrounding offsets carry the mat forward. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; it is a vigorous, reliable grower well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and wall crevices.

common_name: Sir William Lawrence Hens and Chicks (AGM Maroon-Tipped Calcareum Houseleek)

planting.note: Press offsets onto well-drained, ideally slightly alkaline gritty soil in full sun; like other calcareum selections it tolerates damp winters better than most sempervivums.

directions: A selection of the lime-loving Sempervivum calcareum, this cultivar earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2008 for its reliably intense coloring. Small, fleshy grey-green rosettes are tipped in deep maroon-red year round, an effect that deepens rather than fades under stress, and the plant offsets generously on stolons to form dense, slowly spreading clumps. Clusters of sticky, pale green flowers flushed purple appear on short stems in summer. Site it in a rock garden, scree bed, or trough with gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, protecting the crown from standing winter wet.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society (Award of Garden Merit)
Mountain Crest Gardens — Sempervivum Cultivar Guide

common_name: Blue Waves Echeveria (Reinelt Wavy-Margined Teal Hybrid)

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in gritty succulent mix in full sun; strong light intensifies the teal-to-red color shift along the wavy leaf margins.

directions: Bred by Frank Reinelt at the Vetterle and Reinelt Nursery in Capitola, California, 'Blue Waves' is a sister seedling to the similarly popular 'Blue Curls', though its exact parentage was never recorded. Its spoon-shaped, heavily powdered teal-blue leaves develop pronounced wavy margins with age and flush red at the edges in strong sun. Tall, branching flower stalks carry reddish-orange, bell-shaped blooms well above the foliage in summer. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: UC ANR — Under the Solano Sun

common_name: A Grim One Graptoveria (Grim Pun-Named Blue-Green Hybrid)

planting.note: Root leaf or offset cuttings in gritty mix in full sun; give excellent drainage and only moderate water.

directions: This Graptopetalum x Echeveria hybrid was bred by Bob Grim of San Jose, California, and carries a punning name after its breeder. Tight rosettes of thick, pale blue-green leaves take on pink tones at the tips and margins when grown in bright light, forming clusters up to 5 inches across. In late spring, branching flower stalks bear small yellow blooms marked with red spots. Give it full sun and sharp drainage; like most graptoverias it needs only moderate water and propagates readily from leaf cuttings or rooted offsets.

common_name: Fuji Variegated Chinese Dunce Cap (White-Margined Orostachys)

planting.note: Plant offsets into very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; give winter protection in a cold frame or container in colder zones since variegation reduces vigor and cold tolerance versus the straight species.

directions: This variegated sport of the Chinese dunce cap carries creamy white margins around pale blue-green rosette centers, closely mirroring the hens-and-chicks growth habit of the straight species. As with Orostachys generally, each individual rosette is monocarpic and sends up a conical, densely flowered spike before dying back, while offset rosettes continuously replace it to keep the colony going. Because reduced chlorophyll makes variegated forms noticeably less cold-hardy and vigorous than plain-leaved Orostachys iwarenge, it is best grown in a trough or container that can be moved under cover for winter in zones colder than about 7. Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to partial shade, and propagate by separating offset rosettes during the growing season.

planting.note: Propagate by separating rooted branch offsets in spring and setting them into fast-draining, rocky soil; avoid touching or wetting the thick white waxy coating that protects the leaves.

directions: Endemic to the fog-shrouded northern end of Cedros Island off Baja California, this species carries the thickest leaves of any Dudleya, each coated in a heavy white, powdery wax that should never be touched or rinsed off since it shields the plant from intense sun. Over time it develops a stout basal stem that branches into multiple rosettes, slowly forming a clump up to 2 feet wide. Like its relatives it goes dormant and may shrink somewhat during peak summer heat, so water sparingly then and more generously during the cooler growing season. Because wild populations are heavily poached for the collector trade, only acquire nursery-propagated plants, and grow in a fast-draining rocky mix on a slope or in a container.

common_name: San Quintin Liveforever (Baja Red-Flowered Chalk Dudleya)

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring and plant into fast-draining, rocky soil; leave the chalky white farina on the leaves undisturbed.

directions: Native to the San Quintin volcanic field and adjacent Isla San Martin in Baja California, this large, chalky-white Dudleya is one of the few species in the genus adapted almost exclusively to hummingbird pollination, producing long, pendent, red tubular flowers in spring and summer rather than the typical star-shaped blooms. Leaves and flower stalks alike are coated in a protective white, powdery bloom that should not be touched or washed off. Grow in sun to bright shade with occasional to low water, siting it where rainfall and irrigation drain away instantly from the crown. Propagate from rooted offsets, keeping water minimal during its summer dormancy.

common_name: Todos Santos Liveforever (Baja Island Cushion Dudleya)

planting.note: Divide branching stem clusters in spring and plant into fast-draining, rocky soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: A rare and little-cultivated species restricted to the Todos Santos Islands and a single coastal locality in Baja California, Mexico, it grows in a distinctive caespitose habit: slightly sticky-leaved rosettes sit atop elongated, branching stems that gradually build dense cushions up to 16 inches across. Its bell-shaped flowers open white with spreading petals, a departure from the brighter yellow or red blooms of many relatives. Culture follows the same rules as other chalky Dudleya species: sharp drainage, full sun to light shade, and minimal water during summer dormancy. Propagate by dividing rooted stem clusters or rooting stem cuttings.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring and set into fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Endemic to coastal bluffs and slopes of California's San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties, Palmer's liveforever forms a broad basal rosette up to 8 inches wide of pale-to-bright green, lance-shaped leaves often tinged pink. A tall, branching pink-to-green flower stalk carries up to 40 small yellow-to-red or pink blooms in late spring. Like other coastal Dudleya it is summer-dormant and should be kept nearly dry through that period, resuming active growth with the cool, moist fall and winter season typical of its native range. Grow in sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to light coastal shade.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; it multiplies quickly into dense bouquets of small rosettes.

directions: Native to rocky slopes in Turkey, this frost-hardy Rosularia forms compact rosettes of slightly elongated, bright light-green leaves that blush reddish at the edges in strong sun. The entire leaf surface is covered in a short, thick, whitish down that gives the plant a velvety, softly reflective appearance and helps protect it from intense light. It multiplies readily from offsets, quickly forming dense, multi-headed clusters, and produces small pink flowers in June and July. Grow in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun in a rock garden, wall crevice, or alpine trough.

planting.note: Divide and plant rooted sections in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; it spreads readily to form a low groundcover mat.

directions: Native to the Russian Far East and neighboring mountains of East Asia, this low, mat-forming stonecrop carries narrow green leaves that often flush bronze-red in cool fall and winter weather. Abundant clusters of small, star-shaped yellow-to-orange flowers cover the mat in summer and are highly attractive to bees. It is semi-evergreen in mild climates but may die back to the crown in harsh winters, resprouting reliably in spring. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun as an edging plant, rock garden groundcover, or green roof component.

planting.note: Divide and plant rooted stems in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; it trails nicely over rock walls and trough edges.

directions: Native to high mountain ranges of Central Asia including the Altai, Tian Shan, and western Himalaya, this deciduous stonecrop forms a low mound of decumbent stems lined with thick, rounded, pale blue-green leaves. Clusters of small, star-shaped pink to purplish-red flowers appear above the foliage in late summer. It dies back to the crown each winter and regrows vigorously in spring, making an excellent trailing subject over rock walls or spilling from trough edges. Grow in a well-drained site in full sun; this species is also commonly listed in the trade under the name Hylotelephium ewersii.

common_name: Dwarf Tree Stonecrop (Mexican Lava-Field Woody Sedum)

planting.note: Root semi-woody stem cuttings in gritty mix in spring; established plants need only occasional summer water and sharp drainage.

directions: One of the only truly tree-forming members of the genus, this Mexican native develops a thick, stubby woody trunk and upright branching stems that give mature specimens a bonsai-like silhouette over many years. It is native to volcanic lava fields on the central Mexican plateau, where it drops its small, notched green leaves during the dry season and re-leafs with the return of rain. Fragrant, pale yellow flowers blushed pink at the center appear in summer. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water only occasionally in summer; established plants tolerate brief cold snaps into the high teens Fahrenheit.

common_name: Wormleaf Stonecrop (Pacific Northwest Native Yellow-Flowered Sedum)

planting.note: Divide and plant rooted offsets, or direct sow in fall, into gritty, rocky soil in full sun; it naturalizes readily in cliff and talus-like conditions.

directions: Native to rocky cliffs, talus slopes, and ridges from British Columbia and Alberta south to northern California and Wyoming, this exceptionally cold-hardy stonecrop forms low mats of narrow, linear to three-lobed succulent leaves. Bright yellow, sometimes red-veined, star-shaped flowers appear in spring and summer and are an important nectar source, supporting dozens of native bee and butterfly species. It is extremely drought- and cold-tolerant once established in gritty, rocky soil. Use it in naturalistic rock gardens, scree plantings, or xeriscape beds in colder climates where many succulents struggle to overwinter.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright, indirect light; plant slightly deeper than usual to mimic its naturally part-buried habit.

directions: Restricted in the wild to a small area near Calitzdorp in South Africa's Western Cape, this variety of Horse's Teeth Haworthia differs from the typical form in arranging its thick, flat-tipped leaves in a spiraling dome rather than two opposite rows. Each leaf tip is truncated and translucent, forming a window that admits light to the chlorophyll-rich tissue below while most of the plant sits nearly buried in gritty soil in habitat. Its distinctive dome shape, resembling a small stone formation, makes it a favorite among collectors. Grow and water exactly as for the species: bright indirect light, mineral-rich fast-draining mix, and water only once the soil is completely dry.
